content: MARCH5, also referred to as membrane-associated RING-CH-type finger 5, is an enzyme encoded by the MARCH5 gene in humans. This enzyme is localized to the outer membrane of mitochondria and contains four transmembrane domains. The human MARCH5 protein, an E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase, belongs to the transmembrane RING-finger protein family. It has a molecular weight of 31 kDa and consists of 278 amino acids. The protein features an N-terminal zinc-finger domain spanning amino acids 6 to 75 and four C-terminal transmembrane regions. As an E3 ubiquitin ligase, MARCH5 facilitates the transfer of ubiquitin from an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme to specific protein substrates. It was initially identified as a binding partner for mitofusin 2 and dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1). MARCH5 promotes the ubiquitination of Drp1, and its knockdown via RNA interference results in abnormal mitochondrial fusion. Additionally, MARCH5 interacts with mitofusin 1, reducing its levels during certain phases of the cell cycle. By regulating the proteostasis of Drp1, mitofusin 1, and mitofusin 2—key regulators of mitochondrial fusion and fission—MARCH5 plays a critical role in maintaining normal mitochondrial morphology. Deficiencies in MARCH5 function can lead to cellular senescence. From a clinical perspective, MARCH5, also known as MITOL, is thought to protect against nitrosative stress-induced disruptions in mitochondrial dynamics, including morphological stability and mitochondrial transport. This protective role is particularly relevant as MITOL expression decreases with aging in normal tissues, suggesting that it may regulate aging by controlling mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Pathologically, in neuronal cell models, dominant-negative MARCH5 prevents mitochondrial fragmentation during neurodegenerative stress caused by neuron-specific reactive oxygen generators such as 6-hydroxydopamine, the complex I inhibitor rotenone, or Alzheimer’s disease-related amyloid-beta peptide. MARCH5 is also implicated in the removal of proteins associated with neurodegenerative disorders, such as ataxin-3 in Machado–Joseph disease and mutant SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, thereby supporting mitochondrial function. Furthermore, MARCH5 has been linked to toll-like receptors (TLRs), which recognize distinct pathogen-associated molecular patterns and play a crucial role in the innate immune response. Ubiquitin-dependent degradation pathways, in which MARCH5 is involved, are highly relevant to cancer due to their essential roles in protein quality control, immune response regulation, signal transduction, and cell cycle regulation.
